analysis.one_liner: PFC is a government-owned (Navratna) NBFC that provides long-term project finance to power generation, transmission and distribution companies across India, and now also owns and consolidates REC Limited as its subsidiary.
analysis.whats_happening: On 15 October 2026 the RBI granted its No-Objection Certificate for REC Limited to merge into PFC via an 88:100 share swap, a step that still needs shareholder, NCLT and SEBI approvals before it closes. Q2 FY27 (September 2026 quarter) results are due around 6 November 2026, roughly three weeks away. The stock has been under pressure after brokerages, including Morgan Stanley, cut FY26-29 loan growth estimates on both PFC and REC, citing a widening gap between their loan growth and overall bank credit growth to the power sector.
analysis.plain_terms: Think of PFC as a government-run bank that only lends to power companies - and it is about to absorb REC, another government power lender, into itself. The tension: profits, dividends and loan quality all still look fine, but the stock has fallen about 35% from its 2024 peak because analysts worry the easy growth phase for these power lenders is ending, and because the pending REC merger adds uncertainty about how per-share economics will look once it completes.
analysis.quarters: Q1 FY27 (June 2026 quarter): standalone PAT of Rs 4,745 crore, up 5.4% YoY; consolidated PAT (which includes subsidiary REC) of Rs 8,998 crore, up only 0.2% YoY; total income was flat, down 0.2% YoY. The prior quarter, Q2 FY26 (September 2025): standalone PAT Rs 4,462 crore, up 2.1% YoY; consolidated PAT Rs 7,834 crore, up 9.3% YoY. The standalone-versus-consolidated gap in both quarters is because REC is consolidated into PFC's group numbers, not an accounting restatement - but it means headline PAT growth figures you see quoted can differ sharply depending on which number a source is citing. The flattening in standalone total income is the real signal: loan book growth is cooling.
analysis.performance_read: Over 5 years the stock has returned +274.65% versus the Nifty's +25.27%, and over 3 years +50.69% versus +16.83% - a genuine, large outperformance, not an artifact of the 2016 (2-for-1) and 2023 (5-for-4) stock splits, which are liquidity actions already reflected in this price series and not demergers. But most of that gain was front-loaded into 2023-2024: the stock is down 35.6% from its July 2024 peak of Rs 517.26, and has underperformed the Nifty over the last 3 months (-16.0% vs -4.9%) and 1 year (-12.9% vs -9.5%). The peer REC has fallen even more than PFC over 1 year (-14.3%).
analysis.valuation_read: At a P/E of roughly 4.3x and P/B of roughly 0.8x against an ROE near 26.8%, PFC looks statistically cheap. The 'why' matters more than the 'is it': government-owned lenders to a politically sensitive sector (state power distribution companies) structurally trade at low multiples, and that discount has widened recently because analysts have specifically cut loan-growth forecasts, not because the market has mispriced a healthy, fast-growing lender. Cheap here reflects a growth-slowdown view, not a hidden bargain.
analysis.growth_read: Growth has shifted from steady loan-book expansion to near-stagnation: standalone total income was down 0.2% YoY in the June 2026 quarter, and brokerages have cut FY26-29 loan CAGR estimates for PFC to around 6% from around 9% earlier. Profit growth in recent quarters has come mainly from cost and margin management rather than fresh volume - this is margin-led, not volume-led, and margin-led growth in a lending business tends to run out of room once rate cycles turn.
analysis.health_read: Asset quality is a clear strength: standalone gross credit-impaired assets were 1.11% and net credit-impaired assets just 0.15% as of June 2026, among the best in Indian NBFC lending. Standalone net worth was about Rs 1.09 lakh crore (consolidated about Rs 1.87 lakh crore) against a standalone loan book of about Rs 5.70 lakh crore. Profits are converting into consistent quarterly interim dividends. The dominant risk here is business/sector risk - dependence on state power distribution company reforms and the broader power-sector lending cycle - not balance-sheet or credit risk.
analysis.ownership_read: The promoter is the Government of India, holding 55.99% as of March 2026 - this is state ownership, not a private promoter group, so conventional pledging risk does not apply and no pledging has been reported. Foreign institutional investors hold about 18.3%, mutual funds about 10.1%, insurance about 4.3%, and retail investors about 10.2%. No specific well-known individual or marquee fund investor was identified on the register in the sources checked - if you were expecting one, it is not verified as present.
strengths: Net credit-impaired (NPA) ratio of just 0.15% standalone as of June 2026, exceptional for a lender of this size
TTM dividend yield of 5.63%, with regular quarterly interim payouts (e.g., Rs 3.90/share in August 2026)
5-year shareholder return of +274.65% versus the Nifty's +25.27%
Trades at roughly 4.3x earnings and 0.8x book against a ~26.8% ROE
watchpoints: Loan growth is decelerating - standalone total income fell 0.2% YoY in Q1 FY27, and Morgan Stanley cut its FY26-29 loan CAGR estimate to ~6% from ~9%
Stock down 35.6% from its July 2024 peak and underperforming the Nifty over both 3 months (-16.0% vs -4.9%) and 1 year (-12.9% vs -9.5%)
PFC-REC merger still needs shareholder, NCLT and SEBI sign-off after the RBI NOC (15 Oct 2026) - execution and integration risk remain live until it closes
Business is concentrated in power-sector lending to state discoms, making it sensitive to sector reform and policy decisions rather than pure credit underwriting
analysis.one_thing: The Q2 FY27 results due around 6 November 2026 - specifically whether loan book growth and net interest margin confirm or ease the Morgan Stanley growth-slowdown thesis - alongside progress on shareholder/NCLT/SEBI approvals for the REC merger.
analysis.data_notes: PAT figures cross-checked across HDFC Sky, Angel One, Business Standard, Business Upturn, Free Press Journal and Mercom India; they agree on direction but headline numbers vary depending on whether a source quotes standalone or consolidated PAT (consolidated includes subsidiary REC, which is a normal scope difference, not a restatement). Valuation ratios (P/E, P/B, ROE, ROCE) were sourced from aggregator sites rather than the primary filing and should be verified on Screener. Merger swap ratio (88 PFC shares per 100 REC shares) and the RBI NOC date are sourced from merger-specific press coverage, not a company filing excerpt.
